notes: Georg Balthes (born 9 June 1877, died 5 September 1935), house 16 in the Obergasse, had lost a leg. In 1897 and 1902 he asked the presbytery to play the organ; in 1902 he was allowed to play occasionally during services and every third or fourth Sunday.

After organist Martin Buchholzer died in 1906, Georg Balthes (then house 116, neighbour of Thomas Albrich No. 117) was elected organist by six votes to five over Johann Buchholzer; his contract of 8 December 1906 gave him 52 crowns, a share of the church pasture and exemption from communal labour.

In 1909 the presbytery found organist Georg Balthes's playing wanting but kept him, since he had two children and his wife's six-year-old child to support and was disabled; he was probably already alcohol-dependent. In December 1913 he was removed in favour of Rector Georg Konnerth, who however withdrew out of pity for Balthes's four children.

In 1914, with five children in his house, Georg Balthes's wife left him and fled to her brother in Canada; he then lived unmarried with Sofia Widmann, 16 years younger, and had five more children with her. In 1917 he resigned over pay and was reinstated; he stayed organist until his death in 1935.
From 1914 Sofia Widmann, 16 years younger than organist Georg Balthes, lived with him in an unmarried union (he could not divorce after his wife fled to Canada); they had five children together.

In November 1902 a “Baltes Joh. N.109” spoke for the young men's brotherhood before the church council, accusing its officers of pocketing part of the fines they had collected. If this is him, he was still in Roseln that autumn.

notes: Pastor Alfred Csallner objected when he learned a schoolboy was among the Adjuvanten (brass band), and the presbytery forbade it; in 1924 he clashed with the curator over the band contract and called him to order.

Pastor Alfred Csallner was presented to Roseln on 29 September 1923; the presbytery decided he be fetched from Agnetheln and a feast be held at the parsonage open to everyone. He pushed the building of a new church hall and had a notice about new bells placed in a German-American newspaper.

Through the efforts of Pastor Alfred Csallner (in Roseln 1923-1929) the wedding hall in Roseln was built; he later worked at the Sippenamt and in 1946-1950 served as administrator of the Roseln parish.

In 1925 Pastor Alfred Csallner withdrew a disciplinary complaint against a presbyter (Rochus) after an apology; he also quarrelled with teachers. On 21-22 March 1925 he publicly defended the Saxon notary Johann Schmidt, to whom he was related by marriage, against accusers.

On 3 October 1927 Pastor Alfred Csallner won a lawsuit against the parish over a 1,000 Lei hall-building contribution (the parish owed him over 26,000 Lei salary); he then donated the 1,000 Lei. He held his last presbytery session on 3 August 1929.

Pastor Csallner later also petitioned against the expropriation of the church land, showing he had been in conflict with the Volksgruppe, without success; earlier he had met an interned Roseln man in Târgu Jiu and Turnu Măgurele.

Pastor Alfred Csallner, recently released from an internment camp, was proposed on 23 December 1945 as parish administrator (Pfarramtsverweser) of Roseln and was chairing the presbytery by March 1946.

In February 1946 Pastor Alfred Csallner reported to the bishop and consistory on arbitrary round-ups of Saxon men for forced labour, violence by Roma and gendarmes, and seizure of sacks and pigs in Roseln.

Pastor Alfred Csallner's second tenure in Roseln was burdened by tensions with the widow Lutsch; in autumn 1946 the presbytery urged him to teach the children, and his lessons (e.g. a train trip to the Moon) were fondly remembered.
Pastor Alfred Csallner, himself from Bistritz, led the district relief action for North Transylvanian refugees in 1946 and took a North Transylvanian child into his home besides his own six children.

notes: Adolf Michael Heltmann (1848–1923), born in Birthälm, finished Gymnasium in 1867, studied in Leipzig, taught 13 years in Hungarian, was rector in Fogarasch 1885–1889 and was ordained as elected pastor of Roseln on 3 April 1889 (pastor 1889–1898); he drove the building of the new parsonage and served five years as preacher-teacher for half pay.

At his first presbytery session on 19 April 1889 Pastor Adolf Heltmann founded a parsonage building fund; on 8 January 1890 he offered to serve the preacher post free for five years to save about 2,000 fl. The new parsonage was built 1893 (cornerstone ceremonies, first session held there 26 November 1893).
During Pastor Adolf Heltmann's time in Roseln (1889-1898) the Roseln parsonage was built.

Adolf Heltmann stayed in Roseln until after 18 September 1898, then moved to Galt; he died on 28 June 1923 as pastor of Seiburg, aged 74. He also founded a Christmas-tree foundation (1890) whose interest he decided in 1897 to use for a kindergarten keeper.

In 1895 Pastor A. Heltmann, as chairman of the Roseln presbytery, drafted a vehement point-by-point rebuttal of Orthodox priest Nicolau Babes's complaint to the deputy county prefect, stating that the 4,600 fl. loan was an advance on the 8,000 fl. voted unanimously.

Pastor Adolf Heltmann was chairman of the Schenk district agricultural association; in May 1896 he asked for leave to report at its meeting in Rohrbach, and in July 1897 for six days' leave to represent the community in Oderhellen and Budapest in a matter involving large sums.

notes: Pastor Adolf Lutsch, a native of Urwegen, held his first presbytery session in Roseln on 1 December 1929 and raised the church fathers' honorarium from 30 to 3,000 Lei. In August-September 1930 he married Hildegard Klara Böhme in Leipzig and brought her home.

In a long statement read to the presbytery on 12 December 1941, Pastor Adolf Lutsch said he had devoted twelve years of his ministry in Roseln to the German school and warned that the unconditional transfer of school property to the Volksgruppe endangered the church; he also objected that the Nazi welfare organisation (NSV) was to take over the children's Christmas celebration without Christian hymns.
Pastor Adolf Lutsch, born in Urwegen, was elected to Roseln as a young theology candidate (1929), was elected dean in 1945, and was shot by Russians on 29.07.1945.

Pastor Adolf Lutsch tackled the parish debt in the early 1930s by fund transfers, a potato field for the starch factory, and levies; in 1934 the organ was repaired, he fined youths dancing after midnight 10 Lei (buying a brotherhood flag) and introduced the 'Pfingstkrone' custom on 29 June 1934.
Sofia Löprich née Klockner remembered Pastor Adolf Lutsch as learning his sermons by heart, a loving but strict pastor who made pupils write a maxim on order up to 500 times as punishment.

According to his son Werner Lutsch, Pastor Adolf Lutsch lived hidden for about two weeks in the Zinngießerturm in Schäßburg during the Nazi period (date unknown). He was often ill: sick in Advent 1935, granted leave at Epiphany 1942 to fetch his sick wife, operated on in January 1942, on sick leave for four weeks after Whitsun 1942, and ill again in autumn 1942.
From 1938 Pastor Adolf Lutsch led the Roseln parish out of its debts, helped by the debt-conversion law of the late 1930s; in December 1941 the parish had no arrears in teachers' salaries.

On 12 December 1941 Pastor Adolf Lutsch put a counter-motion: hand over school management to the Volksgruppe but only lease (not give) the school property—the school built in 1936 with teacher's residence (topo no. 316), house and yard No. 110b, the school garden and 10 Joch in the “Habesch”—keeping the former preacher's field (topo no. 727) for the church.

Pastor Adolf Lutsch wrote the minutes of the 12 December 1941 meeting himself; he belonged to the Michaelsbruderschaft (a church renewal brotherhood organised by Konrad Möckel of Kronstadt) and probably sought advice from fellow pastors of the Harbach valley and in Hermannstadt.

Through skilful chairing Pastor Adolf Lutsch carried his second counter-motion on the school transfer on 19 December 1941 by his casting vote (7–7) and defeated Michael Frank's motion 7–5 on 28 December 1941; the book says this strengthened the parish's confidence in him, though the school ultimately had to be handed over at an unknown date.

On 24 May 1945 Dean Adolf Lutsch wrote to district attorney Breckner about getting the instruments back; a certificate issued in Romanian two days before his death confirmed he had opposed Andreas Schmidt's Volksgruppe dictatorship and had filed a disciplinary complaint after a blasphemous song at the Zeiden forest bath on 18 August 1943.

On 28 March 1944 Pastor Adolf Lutsch told the presbytery he had handled administrative matters with the curator during seven months without meetings, and urged the presbyters to lead by Christian example; he was ill again in June, mid-July and early August 1944.

On 6 October 1944 the pastor of Roseln (Adolf Lutsch, as the typed note in the presbytery minutes suggests) asked notary Petru Maniu whether presbytery meetings were allowed; the first presbytery meeting under the new conditions was held on 8 October 1944.
In December 1944 Pastor Adolf Lutsch organised the election of a new church father by ballots handed in after the service to get around the ban on assemblies.
In winter 1944-45 German lieutenant Dieter Ehlers secretly visited Pastor Adolf Lutsch at night in Roseln to borrow books.
Pastor Adolf Lutsch was among those called up for deportation on 14 January 1945 but was spared by a medical certificate.

On 15 April 1945 at the district church assembly in Großschenk, Adolf Lutsch, who had already been acting dean, was elected dean (Dechant); a report under his name in 1945 noted he could not set an example in the land reform because the parsonage land had been expropriated.

On 23 April 1945, while Pastor Adolf Lutsch lay ill, the mayor and notary read him a decree and took over the church hall, the school and the teachers' land; he signed the handover protocol with the curator.

On 25 April 1945 a group of young Roma came to the parsonage with the mayor and confiscated seven church brass instruments by protocol; Pastor Adolf Lutsch and the curator reported to the district consistory that return was hopeless.
Adolf Lutsch had held prayer hours in Roseln every Sunday and Friday evening for years; by 1945 children's services had lapsed, but communion was celebrated monthly with very large attendance.

In 1945 Pastor Adolf Lutsch held the apologetics courses ordered by the consistory with the two female teachers of Roseln; on 30 June 1945 he reported they did not contradict church doctrine but had not reached a living faith.

On Sunday 29 July 1945 Pastor Adolf Lutsch held morning service (sermon on Deuteronomy 4:25-31, 'judgment and rescue') and vespers; that night he was shot dead at the parsonage door by a Russian commando that was searching for a hidden German soldier.

Pastor Adolf Lutsch died 29 July 1945 at 11 pm (registered in Agnetheln 1 August 1945; certificate issued only 28 June 1960), was buried on 1 August 1945 in the Roseln cemetery, and is regarded by the author as a martyr; an obituary by Ernst Jekelius appeared on 20.11.1946.
On 15 April 1945 the district church assembly in Großschenk elected pastor Adolf Lutsch as dean; on 29 July 1945 Pastor/Dean Adolph Lutsch was shot dead.

Pastor Adolf Lutsch (1904-1945) went with the deportees to Agnetheln in January 1945 but was freed by a medical commission; he climbed out of a window of the Agnetheln gymnasium hall saying “Gott hat mir geholfen”. Some villagers wondered whether he had been favoured; the church service register shows he was often ill.
Hildegard Klara Böhme of Leipzig married Pastor Adolf Lutsch in 1930 and came to Roseln; she was received on 28 September 1930 and made efforts to learn both the Saxon dialect and Romanian.

Pastor Andreas Scheiner last mentioned the Bruderschaft in the presbytery minutes in 1958; the minutes 1891–1958 contain about a hundred entries on youth matters.

Andreas Scheiner was presented to the Roseln congregation by Dean Kuno Galter on 14 October 1951 and served about ten years. He had twice been suspended from his ministry for political reasons: under Bishop Glondys over decree 924/1936, and after 23 August 1944 because he had acted as commissary chief counsel of the church under Bishop Staedel.

Andreas Scheiner, previously pastor in Mergeln, was elected pastor of Roseln on 26 August 1951; the farmer who had been quartered in the parsonage fetched him and his family from Mergeln in his long carriage.

Pastor Andreas Scheiner met a Ministry of Cults envoy in 1955 and around 1957 co-founded the cooperative 'Înfrăţirea' with Martin Albrich, serving as its cashier; its members were forced into the collective farm around 1960. His wife was elected the first woman presbyter in 1956.

Pastor Andreas Scheiner held the harvest festival on 13 November 1960 and died unexpectedly of a stroke at 5 p.m. the next day, 14 November 1960, in his 71st year; the administrator Schullerus called him 'one of the best in our ranks'.
Andreas Scheiner, a very popular pastor of Roseln respected across the church, was the predecessor of Wieland Graef (1962); his widow stayed on in the parsonage.
Berchta Scheiner née Forfota emigrated from Roseln to Germany shortly before 20 June 1965; after that the parsonage was lived in only by pastors' families.

Michael Töpfer served in the Romanian army until he was to be taken for deportation to Russia; helped by superiors he fled home and had to stay hidden for three years, surviving nightly house searches in which the hay was stabbed with pitchforks. His daughter, eleven in 1945, did not know for two years that he was in the house. By 1948 he could return to normal life, probably helped by the 1948 communiqué; as a Romanian army veteran he was entitled to four hectares of land.
Michael Töpfer, church father, and his wife the church mother supported Pastor Wieland Graef in 1962–64 and were godparents of his first son Herbert.

notes: Michael Zikeli was pastor of Roseln from 14 August 1827 to 5 July 1875; records of marital-dispute hearings from his time run from 23 June 1848 to 7 October 1873.

WP.en: The site has proved itself over centuries. The old settlement was built between gentle hills: the Obergasse, in the background on the left the Romanian church and the Sandberg.
WP.de: Die Lage hat sich über Jahrhunderte bewährt. Zwischen sanften Hügeln wurde die alte Siedlung errichtet: die Obergasse, im Hintergrund links rumänische Kirche und Sandberg.

WP.en: The whitewashed wall of the Lutheran church stands in sharp contrast to the church tower, the former residential tower of the Gräfen, which was built of river stones and quarry stones.

WP.sub: Lutheran church and tower, south side

WP.en: For centuries this church was a bulwark against heathendom and a protection of the Christian German way of life. What will its future be?
WP.de: Jahrundertelang war diese Kirche Bollwerk gegen das Heidentum und Schutz der christlichen deutschen Lebensart. Wie wird ihre Zukunft sein?

WP.en: In Drabenderhöhe there now stands a “Tower of Remembrance”. Inside it are stacked stones from Transylvanian fortified churches – a small fragment of homeland for those who moved away.
